units.tr: Homer sings of the mighty Hector and of brave Achilles; Virgil proclaims the arms of the Phrygian leader.

units.la: Nos Christi insignem multa pietate ministrum, Insignem multa dicimus arte virum:
units.tr: We call him, a minister of Christ remarkable for great piety, a man remarkable for great skill.

units.la: Qui viuens docuit nos rectè viuere: mundo Excedens docuit nos, benè posse mori.
units.tr: Living, he taught us to live rightly; departing from the world, he taught us that one can die well.

units.la: Eximia hæc laus est: quam si quis captat, eodem Ad metam cursu, quo VVidebramus, eat.
units.tr: This is an outstanding praise. Whoever seeks it, let him run to the goal by the same course by which Widebram ran.

units.la: Optatum monstrabit iter sermone diserto Grynæus, Sacri pars & decus & chori.
units.tr: Grynaeus, with eloquent speech, will show the desired way; he is a part and an ornament of the sacred choir.

units.tr: Just as he once published him by voice, so now he publishes him in books, and that under your auspices, noble mind.

units.la: PROGRAMMA. RECTOR ACADEMIAE HEIDELBERGENSIS, EBERHARDVS Comes Solmensis et Dominus in Müntzenberg & Sonnenwalde/ omnibus omnium ordinum Doctoribus, Candidatis & to- ti studiosæ Iuuentuti S. P. D.
units.tr: PROGRAMME. THE RECTOR OF THE UNIVERSITY OF HEIDELBERG, EBERHARD, Count of Solms and Lord of Münzenberg and Sonnenwalde, to all Doctors of every faculty, to the candidates, and to the whole studious youth, greeting and well-wishing.

units.la: HERI manè, febre hectica consumtus, piè & placidè obijt, vir Reuerendus, & omnium bonorum memoria & amore dignissimus D. Fridericus VVidebramus, S. Theologiæ excellentissimus & orthodoxus Doctor: qui quum per omnem vitam suam piè, justè & temperanter vixerit: & in vitæ suæ catastrophe, fidem erga Dominum Iesum Christum, charitatem erga totam Ecclesiam, constantiam in veritatis professione, patientiam & alias virtutes, sic omnibus qui eum inuisere solebant, probauerit, vt nemo non cum fructu sanctum senem & intueretur & alloqueretur: dignissimus enim verò est, cuius exequias sua præsentia exornent omnium Professionum homines.
units.tr: Yesterday morning, consumed by a hectic fever, there died piously and peacefully the Reverend man, worthy of the remembrance and love of all good people, Dr. Friedrich Widebram, most excellent and orthodox Doctor of Sacred Theology. Since he lived piously, justly and temperately throughout his whole life, and in the close of his life showed such faith towards the Lord Jesus Christ, such love towards the whole Church, such constancy in professing the truth, such patience and other virtues, that everyone who was accustomed to visit him left having both seen and spoken with the holy old man with profit; he is indeed most worthy that the men of all faculties adorn his funeral with their presence.

units.la: Hortor itaque Academiæ huius Doctores & Professores, illustratam Nobilitatem, studiosam Iuuentutem, vt frequentes paulò ante secundam horam pomeridianam accedant, ad ædes, in quibus eximius hic Dei seruus postremos suæ vitæ dies, sanctè & cum desiderio migrandi ad Christum, cui vixit & mortuus est, clausit. Benè valete. Perscriptum 3 Maij. 1585.
units.tr: I therefore urge the Doctors and Professors of this University, the illustrious nobility and the studious youth, to come in numbers shortly before two o'clock in the afternoon to the house in which this outstanding servant of God closed the last days of his life, holily and longing to depart to Christ, whom he served and in whom he died. Farewell. Written 3 May 1585.

units.la: ILLVSTRIS & Magnifice D. Rector, Idemque generose Comes: clarissimi Patres & Doctores Academici, heroica Nobilitas, amplissimi Hospites, studiosissima Iuuentus:
units.tr: Illustrious and Magnificent Lord Rector, and you, noble Count, most distinguished Fathers and academic Doctors, heroic nobility, honoured guests, most studious youth:

units.la: Quanquam hoc nouissimo vltimæ Dei patientiæ tempore, neq; veritas, neq; innocentia ipsa, quicquam, seu publicè seu priuatim, profiteri potest: quod non in dubium vocare, aut theonino dente calumniando arrodere ausit tragicus aliquis, suiq; fati immemor, Theocrines, cui ne quidem cum Sanctorum virorum in Christi Iesu sinu quiescentium memoria luctari, religio est: quia tamen nos decet, non vinci ab eo quod est malum, sed bonitate malitiam vincere: & supersunt bonæ Naturæ, quæ delectantur virtutum exemplis & elogiis, haudquaquam illibenter nonnulla dicam, de viri clarissimi & integerrimi, D. FRIDERICI VVIDEBRAMI, S. Theologiæ Doctoris orthodoxi, vitæ & ministerii, quo, Dei consilio seruiens, piè defunctus est, curriculo & periodo.
units.tr: Although in this latest time of God's final patience neither truth nor innocence itself can profess anything, publicly or privately, without some tragic man, forgetful of his own fate, daring to call it into doubt or to gnaw at it with a Theonine tooth by slander, a Theocrines who does not even scruple to contend with the memory of holy men resting in the bosom of Christ Jesus, nevertheless, since it becomes us not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good, and since there remain good-natured people who delight in examples and praises of virtue, I will say a few things, not unwillingly, about the course and conclusion of the life and ministry of the most distinguished and upright man, Dr Friedrich Widebram, orthodox Doctor of Sacred Theology, who, serving the counsel of God, died piously.

units.la: Quum autem mihi nequaquam dubium sit, de omnium vestrum præstanti tùm iudicio, tùm voluntate: non vtar longo proœmio: sed, in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, initium faciam ab ea Dauidis Regis & Prophetæ sanctissimi, sententia, diuinitus inspirata, cuius illustre exemplum, historia de vita, ministerio, & pio obitu Doctoris V. Videbrami, nobis subministrat.
units.tr: Since I have no doubt at all about the outstanding judgement and goodwill of you all, I will not use a long preface. Instead, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I will begin with that saying of King David and most holy Prophet, divinely inspired, of which the life, ministry and pious death of Doctor V. Widebram provides us with a notable example.

units.la: Iustus vt Palma germinabit: vt Cedrus in Libano succrescet cum augmento. Plantati in domo Iehouæ, in atriis Dei nostri florebunt. Psal. 92. 11. 12.
units.tr: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon. Those who are planted in the house of the LORD shall flourish in the courts of our God." Ps. 92. 11, 12.

units.la: Vt enim Palma arbor est ἐμπεδόφυλλον, hoc est, frondibus perpetuò virens: vt impositis ponderibus neutiquam cedit: vt cultellato cortice difficilis est ascensu, fructus autem suauissimos profert: vt denique certaminibus sacris communes subministrat coronas: Ita hic vir longè optimus, per omnem vitam virescente laboribus, vulneribusque, virtute excelluit: cruce Christi in humeros sublata, ea quæ sursum sunt quærens, Dominum strenuè sequutus est: Mundo blandienti δυσπῆξόσοσ, fructus dulcissimos Spiritus sancti, charitatem, gaudium, pacem, lenitatem, benignitatem, bonitatem, fidem, mansuetudinem, temperantiam, fructuosus ijs quibus cum vixit, protulit: & iam cœlestis illius coronæ particeps factus est.
units.tr: For the palm is a tree that is ἐμπεδόφυλλον [always in leaf], that is, always green with fronds; it does not give way under heavy loads; its bark is scored and hard to climb, yet it bears the sweetest fruit; and finally it supplies the common crowns of the sacred contests. So this man, by far the best, flourished in virtue through his whole life, green amid labours and wounds. Bearing the cross of Christ upon his shoulders, seeking the things that are above, he followed the Lord vigorously. Unyielding to a flattering world [δυσπῆξόσοσ], he bore for those among whom he lived the sweetest fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, gentleness, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness and self-control. And now he has become a sharer in that heavenly crown.

units.la: Vt etiam Cedrus, carie vetustateque consumi nescia, inter æternas materias, vt Plinius loquitur, commemoratur: ac teste Dioscoride, succum subministrat crassum, pellucidum & mirè odoratum, qui mortua corpora seruat incorrupta: Ita VVidebramus noster, cum Christo Iesu καλλιελαίῳ plantatus ita coaluit, vt huius virtutis viuifico, lucidissimo & fragrantissimo succo, in sese deriuato recreatus, illuminatus & perfusus, gustum æternæ vitæ superstes in hac mortali vita perciperet: & sese ad Christum per ἐυθανασίαν optatam migrare cupere: ac ad beatam ἀθανασίαν contendere, etiam in vltimo suo agone, sæpenumero profiteretur.
units.tr: The cedar too, which cannot be consumed by rot or age, is recorded, as Pliny says, among eternal materials; and, according to Dioscorides, it yields a thick, transparent and wonderfully fragrant resin which keeps dead bodies uncorrupted. So our Widebram, planted with Christ Jesus [καλλιελαίῳ], grew so firmly into him that, refreshed, illumined and steeped in the life-giving, most bright and fragrant sap of that virtue drawn into himself, he tasted in this mortal life the savour of eternal life that remains, and he often declared, even in his last struggle, that he longed to pass over to Christ by a desired euthanasia [ἐυθανασίαν] and to strive towards blessed immortality [ἀθανασίαν].

units.la: Hæc nimirum eorum est optatissima beatitas, qui plantati in domo Iehouæ, florent in atrijs Dei nostri: qui domestici Dei & Sanctorum conciues sunt: qui denique Iehouam timent, & in vijs eius ambulant.
units.tr: This is surely the most desired blessedness of those who, planted in the house of Jehovah, flourish in the courts of our God; who are the household and fellow-citizens of God and the saints; who, finally, fear Jehovah and walk in his ways.

units.la: Cleobulus apud Diogenem Laertium, nimis vere affirmat, quosdam patriæ dedecori esse, quibusdam autem patriam esse dedecori. Felices ergo sunt ij, quibus patria bene morata ornamento est, & qui eidem ornamento sunt.
units.tr: Cleobulus, in Diogenes Laertius, says with great truth that some are a disgrace to their country, and that for others their country is a disgrace. Happy, therefore, are those by whose good conduct their country is adorned, and who are an adornment to it.

units.la: In horum numero & noster Doctor VVidebramus est, qui anno Epochae Christianae 1532, 4 die Iulij (quo ipso die tredecim annis ante, D. Lutheri & Eccij Disputatio, Lipsiae haberi coepit) Pesneceij, Voitlandiae oppido haud quaquam incelebri, natus, gloria nominis sui, patriae celebritatem auxit. Prima tamen patriae laus ab Ecclesia, communi fidelium patria, cuius ciuem esse praecipua laus est, vt ait Basilius, Dei beneficio, eidem est concessa.
units.tr: Our Doctor Widebram is among their number. He was born on 4 July in the year of the Christian era 1532 (the very day thirteen years earlier on which the disputation of Luther and Eck began at Leipzig), at Pesneceij, a town in Voigtland by no means unknown, and by his renown he increased the fame of his homeland. Yet the first praise of his homeland, namely the Church, the common mother country of the faithful, of which to be a citizen is the chief praise, as Basil says, was granted to him by the goodness of God.

units.la: Vt autem omnia humana ξυμμικτα sunt, & temperamento rerum tristium ac laetarum constant, ac fere plus aloës quàm mellis habent: & verè dicitur in vetere versu: Ipsa dies quandoque parens, quandoque nouerca est: Sic annus ille, tristis quidem fuit obitu Illustrissimi & pientissimi Principis, Ioannis, Ducis Saxoniae, Electoris, qui ante biennium vnà cum aliis quibusdam Principibus, Augustae, in Comitijs, Fidei suae Confessionem, Carolo V. Imperatori Augusto, obtulerat: laetus verò & auspicatus, pacis publicae beneficio nostris Principibus & Magistratibus à Caesare concesso, donec generale, liberum & Christianum Concilium celebraretur. Hanc autem impetrasse perhibentur, Albertus Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, idemque Marchio Brandeburgensis, & Ludouicus Comes Palatinus, Electores; quibus duobus Principibus superstitibus, bellum ob religionem nostris non est illatum, quòd essent quasi publici ἐιξηνοποιοὶ in Germania nostra.
units.tr: But since all human things are mixed, and consist of a blending of sad and joyful events, and nearly always hold more aloes than honey, and since the old verse rightly says, "Day itself is sometimes a mother, sometimes a stepmother," so that year was indeed sad for the death of the most illustrious and most pious Prince John, Duke of Saxony and Elector, who two years before, together with certain other princes, had presented his Confession of Faith at Augsburg to the Emperor Charles V. Yet it was also joyful and auspicious, through the public peace granted to our princes and magistrates by the Emperor until a general, free and Christian Council should be held. It is said that this was obtained by Albert, Archbishop of Mainz and likewise Margrave of Brandenburg, and by Louis, Count Palatine, both electors; and because these two princes were still living, war was not waged on our people for religion, since they were, as it were, public peacemakers in our Germany.

units.la: Natus est autem Doctor VVidebramus, honestissimis parentibus, Bonifacio VVidebramo patre, & matre Anna Stappia, quæ fuit filia, Consulis eius Oppidi Friderici Stappij.
units.tr: Doctor Widebram was born of most honourable parents: his father was Boniface Widebram and his mother Anna Stapp, daughter of Friedrich Stapp, consul of that town.

units.la: Quod si verum est illud Platonis, Quales sunt filij, talis est & domus gubernatio: & illud Euripidis: Filij mares sunt columnæ familiarum: bene morata m fuisse oportet eam familiam in qua is natus est & educatus, qui & habuit cur de honestate parentum gloriaretur, & hoc præstitit, vt grandæua parens, sibi tali pietate & ingenio filium esse, gratularetur. Vtinam vero Iuuentus, tanti viri exemplo admonita, non memoria tantum, sed etiam benefactis id repetat, quod præclarè dixit Ioannes Chrysostomus: Iustius est vt de te glorientur Parentes, quàm tute de parentibus.
units.tr: If it is true, as Plato says, that "such as the children are, such is the management of the household," and as Euripides says, "Sons are the pillars of families," then the family in which he was born and brought up must have been well-mannered, one which had reason to glory in the honesty of its parents, and which brought it about that his aged parent rejoiced to have a son of such piety and talent. Would that young people, reminded by the example of so great a man, might not only remember but also repeat by their deeds what John Chrysostom said well: "It is more just that parents should glory in you than you in your parents."

units.la: Patrem, VVidebramus noster admodum puer, non amisit, sed ad cælestem vitam & consuetudinem præmisit: ac ipse, ab avo materno educatus, quòd ingenio esset [illegible, ~2 letters], ad studia literarum adhibitus fuit, in patria primùm, mox Neobyrgi & demum Isennaci: in qua urbe tum temporis egregij formandæ pueritiæ & adolescentiæ artifices, & tanquam [illegible, ~3 letters], Medlerus & Rosinus, florebant. Quòd autem hisce duobus Præceptoribus eius indoles & ingenium probaretur, & ipse sibi non deesset, felix fuit pueritiæ illius institutio, & disciplina seuerior, quę firmat ingenia, & apta reddit magnis conatibus: vt ait Seneca.
units.tr: Our Widebram did not lose his father while he was still a boy, but sent him ahead to the heavenly life and fellowship. Brought up by his maternal grandfather, and because he was [illegible] in talent, he was set to the study of letters, first in his native town, then at Naumburg, and at last at Eisenach. In that town at that time there flourished the excellent craftsmen of forming boyhood and youth, Medler and Rosinus, as it were [illegible]. Since his character and talent were approved by these two teachers, and since he himself did not fail, that boyhood training was happy, and the stricter discipline which strengthens minds and makes them fit for great efforts, as Seneca says, was of benefit to him.

units.la: Quum autem nimis verè Theophrastus dixerit, admodum difficilè esse de Iuuentute diuinare, quòd ea ætas ferè incerta sit, sine scopo feratur, multisq; mutationibus obnoxia, aliàs aliorsum feratur: Prouidentiæ diuinæ, & ei quidem admodum propitiç, acceptum ferri debet, quòd VVidebramus noster, ætatis suæ anno decimo septimo, Christi Iesu 1549, Ienam Thuringorum, tanquam ad mercatum bonarum literarum missus, optimos eruditae doctrinae & pietatis doctores, & morum gubernatores, Iuuenis sortitus est; & quòd eorundem virtutum exemplo se flecti passus est.
units.tr: Theophrastus said most truly that it is very difficult to divine concerning youth, since that age is largely uncertain, carried without aim, and liable to many changes, now carried one way, now another. To divine providence, and indeed to a most favourable providence, must be credited the fact that our Widebram, in the seventeenth year of his age, in the year of Christ Jesus 1549, sent to Jena of the Thuringians as to a market of good letters, obtained, as a young man, the best teachers of learned doctrine, piety and moral guidance; and that he allowed himself to be bent by the example of those same virtues.

units.la: In horum numero erant, Erardus Sneppius, S. Theologiae D. eximius, cuius in dicendo δεινότητα & ubertatem, illi qui viuum in laudatissima Tubingensi Academia, docentem audierunt, olim non satis celebrare poterant.
units.tr: Among these was Erardus Sneppius, an outstanding doctor of theology, whose skill and abundance in speaking those who heard him teach while he was alive at the celebrated Tübingen Academy could not in former times praise enough.

units.la: Victorinus Strigelius, δευτεραγωνιστὴς, secundum locum obtinebat, vir certè dignus Socratis laude, cuius his verbis meminit Xenophon: μόνον δὲ φάσκειν ἀξίους εἶναι τιμῆς, τοὺς εἰδότας τὰ δέοντα, καὶ ἐξημπνευσαι δυνατὰ μένυς. Solos eos honore dignos iudicabat, qui ea quae oportet sciunt, & rectè eadem oratione sua explicare possunt. Quod enim Senecae consilium sequutus, certis ingenijs sibi immorandum, rectè iudicaret: & Melanchthoniae doctrinę copia, & sermonis sinceritate, & proprietate, perspicuitate, & facilitate delectaretur: sic eum imitari studuit, vt tandem diligentia & exercitio iugi id obtineret, Melanchthonem vt felicissimè in docendo & scribendo repraesentaret.
units.tr: Victorinus Strigelius, the second speaker [δευτεραγωνιστής], held the second place. He was certainly a man worthy of the praise of Socrates, of whom Xenophon speaks in these words: "They say that only those who know what is needful and can explain it are worthy of honour" [μόνον δὲ φάσκειν ἀξίους εἶναι τιμῆς, τοὺς εἰδότας τὰ δέοντα, καὶ ἐξηγήσασθαι δυνατοὺς εἶναι]. Socrates judged that only those deserve honour who know what they ought to know and can set it out properly in their own speech. Following the advice of Seneca, that one should dwell with minds of proven quality, he judged rightly. He delighted in the richness of Melanchthon's teaching, in the purity, propriety, clarity and ease of his language, and so he strove to imitate him, until by diligence and constant practice he came to represent Melanchthon most happily in both teaching and writing.

units.la: Iohannes Stigelius, Poëta & vir optimus tertiū obtinuit locum, tanquā Academicus τριταγωνιστὴς, cuius institutione & exemplo excitatus V Videbramus, naturalem illum impetum ad Poëticen, ardentiorem & firmiorem in sese fieri sentiens, carmen initio componere, tandem etiam magna vbertate suauitateque fundere coepit.
units.tr: Johannes Stigelius, a poet and an excellent man, took the third place, as the third speaker [τριταγωνιστής] in the Academy. Stirred by his instruction and example, Widebram began to write verse, sensing that his natural impulse towards poetry was growing stronger and firmer within him. In time he came to pour it out with great richness and sweetness.

units.la: Biennio post, Iena, in quo oppido eo tempore nondum dū erat Academia priuilegijs instructa, VVitebergam profectus est, vt Philippum Melanchthonem, Germaniæ Phœnicem illum Christianum, audiret. Etsi autem hoc illi cum multis alijs commune fuit: felix tamen præ multis alijs idem fuit, singulari beneuolentia & amore tanti viri; & quòd doctrinam Religionis, quæ ab eodem piè tradebatur, recte didicit. Vt enim Aristoteli perhonorificum fuit, quòd annos viginti Platonem docentem audiuit, eique familiaris fuit: Theophrasto verò Lesbio, & Menedemo Rhodio, quòd Aristotelis γνώριμοι fuissent auditores & σπουδασταί. Ita profecto, & Doctori VVidebramo, magnæ laudi est, quòd laudatissimo & integerrimo viro, D. Philippo, mores, ingenium, harmoniam Musicam & poeticam, ac inprimis veram erga Deum pietatem ita probauit, vt ei charissimus & acceptissimus esset.
units.tr: Two years later he went from Jena, a town which at that time did not yet have an academy furnished with privileges, to Wittenberg, to hear Philip Melanchthon, that Christian Phoenix of Germany. Although this was common to many others, he was more fortunate than many in the singular goodwill and affection of so great a man, and in having learned rightly the doctrine of religion that was piously taught by him. For just as it was most honourable for Aristotle that he heard Plato teaching for twenty years and was his intimate, while it was an honour to Theophrastus of Lesbos and Menedemus of Rhodius that they were acquaintances [γνώριμοι] and disciples [σπουδασταί] of Aristotle, so it is truly a great credit to Doctor Widebram that he so commended himself to that most praiseworthy and upright man, Doctor Philip, by his morals, his talent, his skill in music and poetry, and above all by his true piety towards God, that he became most dear and acceptable to him.

units.la: Magisterij Philosophici honestissimum testimonium (quo magni illi viri, præceptores nostri, Melanchthon, Camerarius, Simon Grynæus, contenti fuerunt) in eadem Academia, Anno Christi 1555, ætatis suæ 22, virtute & doctrina sua assequutus est; quum hoc illi studio esset, quod Anacharsi, qui (vt est apud Diogenem Laërtium) ad Croesum Lydorum Regem scribens, olim testatus est, se ideò Athenis in contubernio eruditorum, quàm Sardibus in aula viuere malle, vt aliquando doctior & melior in patriam redire posset. Vtinam verò hoc ipsum omnibus qui honestissimo studiosorum nomine gaudent, cordi sit.
units.tr: In the same Academy, in the year of Christ 1555, at the age of twenty-two, he obtained by his virtue and learning the most honourable testimony of the Master of Philosophy, the degree with which those great men, our teachers Melanchthon, Camerarius and Simon Grynaeus, were content. He had this aim, the aim of Anacharsis, who, as Diogenes Laertius tells, writing to Croesus, king of the Lydians, once declared that he preferred to live at Athens among learned men rather than at Sardis in the court, so that he might one day return to his homeland more learned and better. Would that this same aim were dear to all who rejoice in the most honourable name of students.

units.la: Sequente anno, ducta Isennaci in vxorem Elizabetha, consulis Ioannis Noëdemi filia, pietatis, pudicitiæ & industriæ Oeconomicæ laude conspicua virgine, maritus factus, de sacro & publico munere, in quo Dei consilio, & aliorum vtilitati, pro eo talento quod à Domino acceperat, seruire posset, cogitare: & legitimam vocationem expetere & expectare coepit. Sunt enim, vt habet Prouerbium: ἀφξονοι Μυσῶν Ξυγαί: expertes inuidentiæ Musarum ianuæ: ac bonæ naturæ, si quod talentum diuinitus sese accepisse animaduertunt, id ad Dei gloriam, & multorum vtilitatem erogare, studio habent.
units.tr: In the following year he married Elizabeth of Isennach, daughter of the councillor Johann Nödemus, a virgin conspicuous for her piety, chastity and domestic industry. Becoming a husband, he began to think about a sacred and public office in which he might serve God's purpose and the benefit of others with the talent he had received from the Lord, and to seek and await a lawful calling. For, as the proverb has it, "the doors of the Muses are free from envy" [ἄφθονοι Μουσῶν θύραι]; men of good nature, when they notice that they have received some talent from God, make it their concern to spend it for the glory of God and the benefit of many.

units.la: Hactenus eam partem vitæ Doctoris VVidebrami breuiter mihi videor delineasse, quæ minus habuit aloës, plus autem mellis: superest, vt ad eam partem accedam, in qua de laboribus, de certaminibus, & de exploratione fidei illius, denique & de pio obitu, breuissime & citra μεμψιμοιρίαν & citra insectationem, mihi agendum erit.
units.tr: So far I seem to have briefly sketched that part of the life of Doctor Widebram which had less of the aloe and more of the honey. It remains that I come to that part in which I must speak, very briefly and without complaint or invective, of his labours, his struggles, the testing of his faith and, finally, his pious death.

units.la: Quum Melanchthon prudentissimo Senatui Seruestano hortator esset, VVidebramus ab hoc ad gubernationem Scholæ, Anno 1557 vocatus, de pueritiæ studijs optimè meritus est; quum, vt ait Fabius, ipse præceptor nec haberet vitia, nec etiam ferret. Quia tamen optimus quisque Præceptor frequentia gaudet: vt idem Fabius testatur: exacto biennio, bona cum omnium pace, Isennacum migrans, sibi delegatum Rectoris in eius oppidi Schola munus suscepit, eoque fideliter per aliquot annos defunctus est.
units.tr: Since Melanchthon was the adviser of the most prudent senate of Zerbst, Widebram, called from there in 1557 to govern a school, deserved very well of the studies of boyhood. As Fabius says, the teacher himself neither had vices nor tolerated them. Yet because every good teacher rejoices in a crowd, as Fabius also testifies, after two years, with the goodwill of all, he migrated to Isennach and undertook the office of rector of the school of that town that had been assigned to him, and he discharged it faithfully for several years.

units.la: Etsi autem imperitis rerum æstimatoribus, humile istud vitæ genus esse videtur, in puluere scholastico versari, & in eo florem ætatis consumere molestum: & indignum homine ingenioso: quia tamen præceptoris opera ad hoc prodest plurimum, vt pueris honesta faciat iucunda: vt Plutarchus alicubi monet, ac vere dixit Cicero: Nullum munus melius maiusúe Reipub. adferre possumus, quàm si doceamus & erudiamus Iuuentutem, ijs præsertim moribus & temporibus, quibus ipsa prolapsa est, vt omnium opibus refrenanda atque coërcenda sit: quantum Respub. Christiana Ludimagistris doctis, ad docendum aptis, laborum tollerantibus, disciplinæ amantibus, debeat, nón certè obscurum est.
units.tr: Although to men unskilled in judging affairs this humble way of life seems to be spent in the dust of the schoolroom, and to waste the flower of one's age in it seems troublesome and unworthy of a man of talent, nevertheless, since the work of a teacher is of the greatest help in making what is honourable pleasant for boys, as Plutarch somewhere advises and Cicero rightly said: "We can bring no better or greater service to the commonwealth than to teach and educate the young, especially in those morals and times into which they have fallen, so that they must be restrained and checked by the efforts of all." How much the Christian commonwealth owes to learned schoolmasters, fit for teaching, enduring of labours and lovers of discipline, is certainly not obscure.

units.la: Vt autem virtus & doctrina in obscuro esse nequeunt: & mediocres honores tempus auget; immodicos abolet, vt prudenter Theopompus Pylijs rescripsit: sic VVidebramus noster super pauca fidelis, super multa autem constituendus, diutius latere non potuit. Vocatus literis publicis Ienâ Thuringorum, in efflorescentem Academiam recens institutam, linguæ Latinæ Professorem egit ex Virgilio & Cæsare: ac Dialecticen, quæ est ὄργανον ὀργάνων & Philosophiæ manus fideliter exposuit: dignus profectò insigni elogio, quo vetustas Epicharmum olim suo merito commendauit:
units.tr: But just as virtue and learning cannot remain in obscurity, and time increases moderate honours while it destroys immoderate ones, as Theopompus wisely wrote back to the Pylians, so our Widebram, faithful in a few things and destined to be set over many, could not remain hidden for long. Called by public letter to Jena in Thuringia, to the newly founded and flourishing Academy, he served as Professor of the Latin language, expounding Virgil and Caesar, and faithfully explained dialectic, which is [ὄργανον ὀργάνων] the organon of organons and the hand of philosophy. He was truly worthy of that distinguished praise with which antiquity once commended Epicharmus for his merit:

units.la: Πολλὰ γὰρ ποτὲ ταῦ ξοὰμ τοῖς παισὶν εἶπε χρήσιμα· μεγάλα χάρις αὐτῷ.
units.tr: "For he once told the boys many useful things; great thanks to him" [Πολλὰ γὰρ ποτὲ ταῦ ξοὰμ τοῖς παισὶν εἶπε χρήσιμα· μεγάλα χάρις αὐτῷ].

units.la: Quòd autem in ea urbe, quidam ἑτεροδιδασκαλοῦντες, parum æqui essent, pridem piè defuncti Melanchthonis doctrinæ & consiliorum æstimatores: atque adeò ijs omnibus, qui hæc probantes, delectabantur memoria virtutum, doctrinæ, & meritorum in Rempub. Christianam tanti viri, infesti essent: factum est, vt humanissimis literis Doctoris Peuceri, doctissimi ac optimi quidam viri, VVitebergam accerserentur, ac eò quoque sese conferrent. In horum numero fuit & Christianus ille clarissimusque Iurisconsultus Germaniæ, Dn. Matthæus VVesenbeccius, & VVidebramus noster; qui illud Ciceronis ad Atticum dictum probans: Nihil bono viro ac quieto magis conuenit, quàm abesse à ciuilibus controuersijs: cedendum sibi τῇ θυμομαχίᾳ & odijs quorundam hominum censuit: sicut sæpe boni viri, ne cum arena luctandum esset, vehementioribus ingenijs cesserunt, ne maiores motus in Ecclesia aut Republica excitarentur.
units.tr: But since in that city certain men teaching otherwise were not well disposed, appraisers of the doctrine and counsels of Melanchthon, who had lately died piously, and were hostile to all who approved these things and delighted in the remembrance of the virtues, learning and services to the Christian commonwealth of so great a man, it came about that certain men of great learning and goodness were summoned to Wittenberg through the learned letters of Doctor Peucer, and went there themselves. Among these was that renowned and Christian jurist of Germany, Doctor Matthaeus Wesenbeck, and our Widebram. Approving Cicero's saying to Atticus, "Nothing suits a good and quiet man more than to be away from civil quarrels," he judged that he must yield to the frenzy of spirit [θυμομαχία] and to the hatreds of certain men, just as good men have often yielded to more vehement natures rather than wrestle in the sand, so that greater disturbances might not be stirred up in the Church or the commonwealth.

units.la: Factum est autem, Anno Christi 1570, vt vnanimi consensu, Ecclesiæ, Senatus & Academiæ VVitebergensis, cura Pastoris eius Ecclesiæ, post obitum Reuerendi & clarissimi viri Doctoris Theologiæ, Pauli Eberi, Domino VVidebramo, serió tantam prouinciam detrectanti, demandata sit. Tanti muneris functionem, quum diu multumq; citra ἀκνισμόν suscipere recusauisset, amplexus tandem fuit cum hac protestatione, vt videlicet cæteri Theologi, si quādo res ita postularet, consilio & auxilio ipsi præstò essent. Non enim solebat ἱσοβασιλεύς, & seipsum solum audire, admirari & efferre: vt faciunt ἰσχυρογνώμονες & ambitiosi homines. Non autem multò post mandatu Illustrissimi Principis Electoris, Saxoniæ Ducis, D. Avgvsti, vnà cum alijs quibusdā doctissimis viris, Theologiæ Doctoris gradu & testimonio est ornatus. In horum numero fuerunt, viri bonorum amore ob virtutem & ὀρθοδοξίαν dignissimi, Henricus Moller, quem doctissimum: Caspar Cruciger, quem acutissimum: Christophorus Pezelius, quem disertissimum: vt VVidebramum nostrum pientissimum grauissimumq;, felicem & sapientem ingeniorum æstimatorem, pronunciasse accepimus D. Pevcervm: cui viro, doctrina & virtute præcellenti, non cum Antisthene, Socratis robur & tolerantiam: sed potius cum Petro Apostolo, virtutem in fide, & mitigationem ærumnarum opto. De cæteris viris clarissimis, qui istorum ξυμπαρασάται & collegæ fuerunt, ideo mihi nihil dicendum censeo; quia vnumquemq; sua suorumq; laude delectari persuasum habens: malim illis apud Christum Iesum bene precando prodesse: quàm apud homines meo encomio molestus esse.
units.tr: Then in the year of Christ 1570 it came about that, by the unanimous consent of the Church, the Senate and the Academy of Wittenberg, the care of the minister of that church was entrusted to Doctor Widebram, after the death of the reverend and most renowned Doctor of Theology, Paul Eber, although he seriously declined so great a charge. He had long and repeatedly refused to undertake the discharge of this office without hesitation [ἀκνισμός], but at last he embraced it, with this protestation: that the other theologians would be at hand to give him counsel and help whenever the matter should so require. For he was not wont to be a co-king [ἱσοβασιλεύς], to hear, admire and exalt only himself, as do the obstinate-minded [ἰσχυρογνώμονες] and ambitious men. Not long afterwards, by the command of the most illustrious Prince Elector, Duke August of Saxony, he was adorned with the degree and testimony of Doctor of Theology, together with certain other most learned men. Among these were men most worthy of the love of good men for their virtue and orthodoxy: Henricus Moller, whom we have heard Peucer call most learned; Caspar Cruciger, most acute; Christophorus Pezelius, most eloquent; and Widebram, whom we have heard Peucer pronounce most pious and most serious, a happy and wise judge of minds. To this man, excelling in learning and virtue, I wish not the strength and endurance of Socrates, as with Antisthenes, but rather the virtue in faith and the mitigation of hardships, as with the Apostle Peter. As for the other most illustrious men who were his companions and colleagues [ξυμπαρασάται], I think nothing should be said here, because I am persuaded that each one delights in his own praise and that of his people, and I would rather help them by praying well to Christ Jesus than trouble men with my encomium.

units.la: Accepi Dominum VVidebramum ingenuè magnis quibusdam in hac vrbe viris fassum esse, se, quum ad Ministerium Ecclesiæ accederet, alienum à sententia, quam de Eucharistia nostræ Ecclesiæ profitentur: hoc tantum habuisse, vt nostros iudicaret odio nō habendos, nec hostilibus anathematismis & virulentis Scriptis insectandos. Sed quum incidisset in quosdam doctos & exercitatos homines, qui ijs argumētis piam nostram doctrinam defendebant, quibus non nisi responsionibus ab ipsomet D. Luthero in polemicis scriptis traditis, satisfieri posse opinatus fuerat: vbi vidisset nullum Argumentum ita solidè ab eodem confutari, paginas interdum ironijs, sarcasmis & alijs inconsultis vocibus respergi: lacrymis præ dolore se paginas illas madefecisse, confitebatur. Fortassis aliquis σειογνώμων sinistrè id interpretaretur. Sed tamen, quum Lutherum Dei seruum, non ita impotenter in conseruos, doctrinâ, si non superiores, certè pares, debacchari & detonare debuisse, serui Christi officium postulet: quis miretur, tùm VVidebramum deplorasse Lutheri infirmitatem: tùm multos modestos & elegantes homines, à nobis admoneti, vt illius viri Scripta polemica legentes, quid de eius doctridoctrina Eucharistica sit statuendum, ex vehementissimæ intemperiei gustu, cognoscant. Vtinam, vtinam homines moderati, qui Lutheri opinionem imbiberunt, Lutheri polemica Scripta legant, & ad analogiam fidei exigant: nec de Lutheri dogmate prius pronuncient, quàm, accuratè illius Scriptis lectis, & cum vel vnico Oecolampadij Dialogo collatis, quid sibi tandem sit statuendum, intellexerint. Nam & illis diu deliberandum, quum semel est statuendum.
units.tr: I have heard that Widebram openly admitted to some distinguished men in this city that when he came to the ministry of the Church he differed from the view of the Eucharist that our Church professes. He had held only this much: that he judged our people were not to be hated, nor attacked with hostile anathemas and venomous writings. But when he fell in with some learned and experienced men who defended our pious doctrine with arguments which he had thought could be met only by the replies that Dr. Luther himself had set out in his polemical writings, and when he saw that no argument was solidly refuted by Luther, and that Luther's pages were sometimes sprinkled with irony, sarcasm and other unseemly words, he confessed that he had wet those pages with tears of grief. Perhaps some ill-natured person would interpret this wrongly. But since the duty of a servant of Christ requires that Luther, a servant of God, should not have raged and thundered so intemperately against fellow servants who were, if not superior in learning, at least equal to him, who would be surprised that Widebram lamented Luther's weakness? Who would be surprised that we have urged many modest and refined men to read that man's polemical writings and to learn, from the taste of his extreme intemperance, what must be decided about his Eucharistic doctrine? Would that moderate men, who have imbibed Luther's opinion, would read Luther's polemical writings, test them by the analogy of faith, and not pronounce on Luther's dogma until they have read his writings carefully, compared them with at least the single Dialogue of Oecolampadius, and understood what must finally be decided. For that too must be deliberated for a long time, once it is to be decided.

units.la: Anno 1572, Dresdam vnà cum optimis & doctissimis Collegis vocatus est V Videbramus, vbi consensu Theologorum, qui tum erant in ditione illustrissimi Electoris Saxoniæ, Formula Consensus Dresdensis deliberata & edita fuit.
units.tr: In 1572 Widebram was called to Dresden, together with excellent and most learned colleagues, where, by the agreement of the theologians who were then within the territory of the most illustrious Elector of Saxony, the Formula of Concord of Dresden was drawn up and published.

units.la: Sequente anno, Thuringiacarum Ecclesiarum inspectioni, vnà cū alijs quibusdam Theologis, interfuit.
units.tr: The following year he took part, together with some other theologians, in the visitation of the Thuringian churches.

units.la: De his omnibus, vt maximè nemo nostrum sibi iudicium sumat: quòd de ijs quæ minùs comperta nobis sunt, minimè nobis sit pronunciandum: ne videlicet calculi nostri præuertant cognitionem: Christianæ tamen charitatis fuerit, omnia in meliore parte interpretari; nec prius de aliorum laboribus, consilijs, dictis, factisq; pronunciare, quàm censoria æstimatione, eaq; seuerissima, erga nosmetipsos defuncti fuerimus.
units.tr: Concerning all these matters, let none of us take judgment upon himself so far as to pronounce on things that are less known to us, lest our votes forestall our knowledge. Still, it is a mark of Christian charity to interpret everything in the better light, and not to pronounce on the labours, counsels, words or deeds of others until we have been most severe in judging ourselves.

units.la: O vtinam nos adsuefaciamus ad eam moderationem & ἐπιείκεια, vt quū de alijs nobis est pronunciandum, initium faciamus à virtutum Deiqúe donorum humanissima inuestigatione, & candidissima æstimatione; nec temerè, nec προπετῶς, nec etiam prius ad reprehensionem vllius vel minimi vitij accedamus, quàm nos ab eo tam longo discrimine abesse rectè collegerimus, quanto à Smaragdo vitrum, ab auro plumbum, abesse intelligimus. Sed hanc moderationem probabunt ij, quibus id dabit is qui dixit, ad confusionem superborum, ad solatium humilium: DISCITE A ME, QVOD MITIS SIM ET HVMILIS CORDE. Matth. 11. 29.
units.tr: O that we might accustom ourselves to such moderation and fairness [ἐπιείκεια] that, when we must pronounce on others, we begin with the most humane investigation and the most candid estimate of their virtues and of the gifts of God. Let us not come rashly, nor hastily [προπετῶς], nor even to the rebuke of any, even the smallest, fault until we have rightly concluded that we are as far from that fault as we understand glass to be from emerald, or lead from gold. But those will approve of this moderation to whom He who said it will grant it, for the confusion of the proud and the comfort of the humble: LEARN FROM ME, FOR I AM GENTLE AND LOWLY IN HEART. Matth. 11. 29.

units.la: Interea dum haec fiunt, Dominus Iesus respexit optimum virum Doctorem VVidebramum, & eodem tempore, veritatis circa rem Eucharisticam fulgorem, mentem eius magis magisq; illustrauit: & eundem veritatis comitem CRVCEM gestare iussit.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while these things were happening, the Lord Jesus looked upon the excellent man, Dr. Widebram, and at the same time illumined his mind more and more with the brightness of the truth concerning the Eucharist, and ordered him to bear that same CROSS as the companion of the truth.

units.la: Praeclare autem Maximus in Sermone de Martyribus dixit: Crux non solum dicitur, quae tempore passionis ligni affixione conficitur: sed quae totius vitae curriculo cunctarum disciplinarum virtutibus coaptatur. Vt non solum intelligatur crux ligni patibulum, sed piae vitae, virtutisq; propositum: unde omnis Christiani vita, qui secundum Euangelium vixerit, crux est atq; martyrium.
units.tr: Maximus, in his sermon on the martyrs, said admirably: The cross is not only that which is made by fixing a body to wood at the time of the passion, but that which is fitted through the whole course of life to the virtues of every discipline. So the cross is understood not only as the wooden gibbet, but as the purpose of a pious life and of virtue; whence the whole life of every Christian who has lived according to the Gospel is a cross and a martyrdom.

units.la: Sequente anno, qui fuit 1574, ob diu multumque denegatam subscriptionem Torgensium Articulorum, De controuersia Eucharistica, vnà cum aliis praestantibus viris, captiuitate, cuius (vt in Epistola quadam ait beatus Hieronymus) nulla maior calamitas est, quàm ad alienam libidinem trahi, & menstruo carcere mulctatus: certis tandem expressisq; conditionibus, quarum testes se fore quidam Lipsenses Theologi, sanctè receperant, eisdem subscripsit. Sed conditiones eae postea (vt mollissimè loquar) ab his neglectae, nec etiam editae fuerunt.
units.tr: In the following year, 1574, on account of his long-refused subscription to the Torgau Articles on the Eucharistic controversy, he was imprisoned along with other excellent men. This captivity (as blessed Jerome says in a certain letter) is no greater calamity than to be dragged about at another's lust and punished with a monthly prison. At last, on certain definite conditions, of which some Leipzig theologians solemnly undertook to be witnesses, he subscribed to them. But those conditions were afterwards neglected by these men (to put it most mildly), and were not even published.

units.la: Mihi sanè de eiusmodi subscriptionibus, quae nunc etiam à Iurisconsultis, à Medicis, à Philosophis exto quentur (vt Scripta quaedam noua, ephemera, maledica in Ecclesias auctoritatem aliquam fidemq; consequantur) cogitanti, sæpenumero in mentem venit Hilarij Pictauiensis, de Concilijs disserétis, oratio memoria dignissima, in qua Gallicanis Ecclesijs eo nomine plurimum gratulatur, quòd nullam aliam nec excudissent, nec recepissent, nec omnino nouissent Consessionem, quàm veterem illam, & simplicissimā, quæ ab æstate Apostolorum apud omnes Ecclesias recepta fuerat. Res enim ipsa loquitur, Formularum istarum, & subscriptionum, si semel Diotrephes vnus aut alter dominari Clero Domini coeperint, nullum finem esse: præsertim si hi Magistratum habeant plus æquo credulum & sibi obsequentem.
units.tr: For my part, when I consider subscriptions of this kind, which are now extracted even from jurists, physicians and philosophers, so that new, ephemeral, slanderous writings may acquire some authority and credit in the Churches, there often comes to mind the discourse of Hilary of Poitiers on the Councils, a most memorable oration, in which he greatly congratulates the Gallican Churches on this account: that they had neither drawn up, nor received, nor known at all any other confession than that old and most simple one which had been received in all the Churches from the age of the Apostles. For the matter itself speaks: once one or two Diotrephes begin to lord it over the clergy of the Lord, such formularies and subscriptions have no end, especially if these men have a magistracy more credulous than is right and compliant with them.

units.la: Post hanc tragœdiam, Naumburgum est relegatus, & per triennium in ea vrbe commoratus, Psalterij ἐμμετρον versionem, quam Christo Domino in carcere vouerat, absoluit. Memini autem me audire versus quosdam de illius in ea vrbe exercitijs priuatis, qui ita habent: Hic studijs miscere preces, lacrymasque solebam, Tristis in exilio quum Videbramus eram. Solus eram, nec eram tamen illo tempore solus: Quando suo mecum numine Christus erat.
units.tr: After this tragedy he was relegated to Naumburg, where he remained for three years, and there he completed the metrical version of the Psalter, which he had vowed to Christ the Lord while in prison. I remember hearing some verses about his private exercises in that city, which go thus: Here I used to mingle prayers with my studies and tears, sad in exile, when I was Widebram. I was alone, and yet at that time I was not alone, when Christ was with me by his divine power.

units.la: Post exactum triennium exulare iussus, (id quod illi & cum alijs bonis commune, & patrimonij causa difficile & singularis damni causa fuit) quum loca quædam adijssel, hospitium tandem honestum, & functionem sanctam obtinuit in valle Deciana, benignissimè eum vocante & tanquam Eliam exulem suscipiente, illustri & præpotente Heroe, D. Ioannes Comite Nassouiensi, cuius ea erat animi tùm magnitudo tùm pietas, vt Christi seruos & testes, nequaquam in cuiusquam alterius Dynastæ gratiam, sibi iudicaret aspernandos: quo nomine & Ipsius excelsitati, & heroicæ posteritati haud dubiè benedicet Deus, eamq; mercede prophetarum ornabit.
units.tr: When the three years were over, he was ordered into exile. This was a common lot for him, as for other good men, and it was a difficult and singular loss on account of his property. After he had gone to several places, he at last obtained an honourable lodging and a holy office in the Deciana valley, where the illustrious and most powerful hero, Lord John, Count of Nassau, invited him most kindly and received him as Elijah was received in exile. Such was the greatness and piety of this man's spirit that he judged the servants and witnesses of Christ were by no means to be spurned for the favour of any other lord. For this God will undoubtedly bless both his excellency and his heroic posterity, and will adorn them with the reward of the prophets.

units.la: Vt autem vir bonus <bl>κοινὸν ἀγαθὸν</bl>, commune bonum est, nec quicquam aliud maiori studio habet, quàm vt multis prosit: ita VVidebramus noster, non tantùm Ecclesiæ, cui tum præesse coeperat, piè tùm docendo tùm viuendo; sed etiam vicinïæ, cùm Ecclesiarum inspectione ipsius fidei & curæ demandata fideliter defungeretur, plurimum profuit.
units.tr: Just as a good man is a common good [κοινὸν ἀγαθὸν] and has nothing he cares for more than to benefit many, so our Widebram was of great service, not only to the Church over which he had begun to preside, teaching and living piously, but also to the neighbourhood, since he faithfully discharged the care and oversight of the Churches entrusted to him for their visitation.

units.la: Anno 1579, rogatu amplissimi Senatus Bremensis, & venia illustris Comitis ac Domini sui, Bremam, vnà cum viro clarissimo, D. Christophoro Pezelio, S. Theologiæ & orthodoxo & disertissimo Doctore, est profectus, ob dissidia quædam inter verbi Dei Ministros tum ibidem gliscentia, quæ, Deo ipsorum consiliis benedicente, vtriusq; diligenti moderatione, studio veri & grauitate simplici, sunt sopita.
units.tr: In 1579, at the request of the most honourable Senate of Bremen, and with the permission of his illustrious Count and Lord, he went to Bremen together with the most distinguished man, Dr. Christoph Pezel, a theologian, orthodox and most eloquent teacher. He went because of certain disputes that were then flaring up among the ministers of God's Word there. With God blessing their counsels, these were calmed by the careful moderation of both men, their zeal for the truth and their plain gravity.

units.la: Quadriennio post, collega Reuerendo & clarissimo viro, Gaspare Oleuiano S. Theologiæ Doctore, Ecclesias in ea ditione Solmensi, quæ subiecta est inclyto & Illustri, magnanimoque Heroi, D. Conrado Comiti à Solms, Braunfels, & Domino in Müntzenberg, reduxit ad synceritatem puritatemq; doctrinæ Apostolicæ, & ceremoniarū primitiuæ Ecclesiæ. Vtinam id in aliis quoq; Ecclesijs, in quibus non paucæ Pontificiæ corruptelæ in ceremonijs & liturgia Sacramentorum reliquæ hæserunt, tandem aliquando præstetur.
units.tr: Four years later, with his colleague, the reverend and distinguished man Gaspar Olevianus, Doctor of Theology, he brought the churches in the Solms territory, which is subject to the famous, illustrious and magnanimous hero Lord Conrad, Count of Solms, Braunfels, and Lord of Münzenberg, back to the purity and sincerity of apostolic doctrine and of the ceremonies of the primitive Church. Would that this might at last be accomplished also in other churches, in which not a few Papist corruptions in ceremonies and in the liturgy of the sacraments have remained.

units.la: Scio ego, quosdam sic acquiescere in rudimentis illis suæ Ecclesiasticæ Reformationis, & in hominum quorundam qui illis tum defuncti sunt, quum obscurior rior adhuc doctrinæ fulgor in eorum mentibus esset, nimia admiratione: vt eos tanquam nouatores accusent, qui nonnulla emendant, quædam etiam abrogant, vt horrendos illos exorcismos in Baptismo infantum: idola, & alia portenta.
units.tr: I know that some people acquiesce so much in those first rudiments of their Church's Reformation, and in the excessive admiration of certain men who died at that time, when the light of doctrine in their minds was still rather dim, that they accuse as innovators those who amend some things and even abolish others, such as those horrible exorcisms in infant baptism, images, and other monstrosities.

units.la: Verum enimuerò, illos cogitare oportebat; prim ò, neq; Lutheri, neq; vllius alterius tantam apud pios authoritatem esse debere, vt eius præiudicio contentos, negligere & institutionem & exemplum primitiuæ Ecclesiæ oporteat: deinde, multò satius esse, si quæ Ecclesia sua vulnera & suos næuos sentiat & agnoscat, & illis medicam manum adhibeat: quàm si lethargo & stupore laborans, sua mala non sentiat, ac proinde nec medicam manum admittat.
units.tr: Indeed, they ought to have considered two things. First, neither Luther nor anyone else should have such authority among the godly that, content with his prejudgment, they must neglect both the teaching and the practice of the primitive Church. Second, it is far better for a Church to feel and acknowledge its own wounds and blemishes and to apply a healing hand to them, than, labouring under lethargy and stupor, to be unaware of its ills and therefore to admit no healing hand at all.

units.la: Vocatus tandem est Doctor V Videbramus, ab Illustrissimo & potentissimo Principe nostro, Duce Iohanne Casimiro, Comite Palatino ad Rhenum &c. Heydelbergam, Anno 1584, vt deliberationibus de Ecclesijs & Scholis rectè regendis, vnà cum alijs quibusdam clarissimis & optimis ac prudentissimis viris, Senatoribus Ecclesiasticis, & interesset & præesset.
units.tr: At last Doctor Widebram was summoned to Heidelberg in 1584 by our most illustrious and powerful Prince, Duke John Casimir, Count Palatine of the Rhine, etc., so that he might both take part in and preside over the deliberations on the proper ordering of the Churches and schools, together with certain other most distinguished, excellent and prudent men, ecclesiastical councillors.

units.la: Memini me audire à Cl. viro, Doctore Io. Iacobo Grynæo, factum, vt cum vtriusq; ipsorum opera, diuersa nonnihil ratione, conducta esset ab Illustrissimo Principe, ac Grynæo Basileam recurrendum esset; V Videbramus hoc Propemtico votiuo ipsum prosequeretur: cuius etiam paulò ante sanctum vitæ huius exitum memoriam refricans, bene precatus est ministerio ipsius Academico, ac Deo gratias egit, quòd sibi datum esset, inter sancta Domini Grynæi (qui ipsum non infrequenter inuisere solebat) colloquia postremos vitæ huius dies claudere: Quos animis dudum iunxit communio Christi, Quàm bene corporibus nunc quoq; iunxit amor! O Grynaee meipars altera pectoris, vnus Dum sumus in Domino spiritus atq; caro. Quàm cupiam vitæ reliquum traducere tecum, Inq; tuo moriens claudere fata sinu: Vt lucrari Animas, de carne & sanguine Christi Falsa refutando, vera probando, queam? Vade, redi incolumis Grynaee, interq; precandum Cum pietate mei nominis esto memor: Donec ab hac turbis ereptos, pace perenni Vnanimes cœli iungat in arce domus:
units.tr: I remember hearing from the distinguished man, Doctor Johann Jakob Grynaeus, that when both of them had been engaged by the Prince, though in somewhat different capacities, and Grynaeus had to return to Basel, Widebram accompanied him with this votive Propemticon. A little before Grynaeus's holy departure from this life, recalling it to mind, Widebram spoke well of his academic ministry and gave thanks to God that it had been granted to him to close his last days of life in the holy conversations of Doctor Grynaeus, who often used to visit him. [The verses follow:] "Whom the communion of Christ long ago joined in spirit, how well love has now joined in body too! O Grynaeus, the other half of my heart, one spirit and flesh while we are in the Lord! How I desire to spend the rest of my life with you, and dying to close my fate in your bosom, so that I might gain souls, refuting falsehoods about the flesh and blood of Christ and proving truths! Go, Grynaeus, and return unharmed; and in your prayers, be mindful of my name with devotion, until the house of heaven, in one accord, joins us in everlasting peace, rescued from these turmoils."

units.la: Accidit autem illi id quod est in vetere prouerbio: Mala senium accelerant.
units.tr: What is said in the old proverb befell him: misfortunes hasten old age.

units.la: Αἱ γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσι.
units.tr: Αἱ γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσι. [For mortals grow old quickly in misfortune.]

units.la: Quippe repente homines curisq; malisq; senescunt.
units.tr: Indeed, men grow old suddenly through cares and troubles.

units.la: Docendi laboribus, curis de Ecclesia, incommodis exilij, iniurijs aduersariorum fractus & confectus, Heydelbergam superiore anno venit: ac tandem hectica febre, ad quam alia quoq; symptomata accesserunt, correptus, toto illo tepore quo decubuit, summisit se instar agni sub potenti manu Dei. De vita æterna, & de sua ad Christum migratione, & cū Grynæo, & cum aliis optimis & clarissimis viris libentissimè colloquebatur.
units.tr: Worn down and exhausted by the labours of teaching, by anxieties about the Church, by the hardships of exile and by the injuries of his adversaries, he came to Heidelberg the year before. At last he was seized by hectic fever, to which other symptoms were added, and throughout the whole time he was confined to bed he submitted himself, like a lamb, under the mighty hand of God. He conversed most willingly about eternal life, about his own passage to Christ, and with Grynaeus and other excellent and distinguished men.

units.la: Cùm ei recitasset Grynæus historiam de Babyla Martyre Antiocheno, qui cum grandæua coniuge, & aliquot filijs ductus esset ad supplicium, & vbi spectator fuisset necis filiorum; ceruicem feriendam præbens dixit: Reuertere anima mea ad requiem tuam, quia Iehouah benefecit tibi: liberasti anima meam à morte, pedem meum à lapsu, oculos meos à lacrymis: ambulabo in luce viuentiu: V Videbramus noster ea valde delectabatur, & recitabat verba Pauli: Cupio migrare hinc, & esse cum Christo: ac testabatur, se desiderio clari conspectus Dei & liberationis a toto peccato, vehementer affici.
units.tr: When Grynaeus had read to him the story of Babylas, the martyr of Antioch, who was led to execution with his aged wife and several sons, and who, having watched the killing of his sons, offered his neck to the axe and said: "Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; you have delivered my soul from death, my foot from falling, my eyes from tears; I shall walk in the light of the living" — our Widebram greatly delighted in these words, and recited the words of Paul: "I desire to depart and be with Christ." He testified that he was deeply moved by longing for the clear sight of God and for deliverance from all sin.

units.la: Rogauit autem aliquoties & ipsum & alios quosdam praestantes viros, ut testes essent sui sermonis, quo professus esset, se iam in actu postremo vitae suae, cum sensu gaudij spiritualis, doctrinam Ecclesiae nostrae de Eucharistia & de Spirituali communione corporis & sanguinis Christi, ad cuius agnitionem sero vocatus esset a Domino, probare: eius cognitionem sibi gratulari: & in ea acquiescentem ad Christum Dominum migrare.
units.tr: He also asked several times both Grynaeus himself and certain other outstanding men to be witnesses to his words, by which he professed that now, in the final act of his life, with a sense of spiritual joy, he was proving the doctrine of our Church concerning the Eucharist and the spiritual communion of the body and blood of Christ, to the knowledge of which he had been called late by the Lord; that he rejoiced in this knowledge, and that, resting in it, he was departing to Christ the Lord.

units.la: Alio quodam die Grynaeo dicebat: Tu vero testis mihi esto, quod sancte in fide Christi Iesu, sim mortuus.
units.tr: On another day he said to Grynaeus: "Be my witness, then, that I have died holy in the faith of Christ Jesus."

units.la: Gratias etiam suo nomine agi voluit, pro beneficijs in se collatis, & Illustrissimo nostro Principi, Duci Iohanni Casimiro, & Illustrissimae eius coniugi, ac huius parenti, Illustrissimo & potentissimo Duci Saxoniae, D. Augusto, Principi Electori.
units.tr: He also wished thanks to be given in his name for the benefits bestowed on him, both to our most illustrious Prince, Duke John Casimir, and to his most illustrious wife, and to her parent, the most illustrious and powerful Duke of Saxony, Lord Augustus, Prince Elector.

units.la: Hoc solum valde querebatur, quod quum eo animo Heydelbergam accessisset, ut regni Christi negotijs promouendis, reliquum vitae tempus optime collocaret, aduersa valetudine praepeditus, minus praestitisset quam volebat. Responsum illi est, magnu quiddam esse Ecclesiae caussa, puras ad Deum attollere manus, concipere pias preces & ΔοξολογίΑς, publico priuatoque nomine Deo gratias agere pro spirituali & corporali benedictione: ac eo nomine & ipsum & alios pios, plurimum prodesse Ecclesiae, etiam quando per valetudinem munia caetera obire non possunt.
units.tr: His only great complaint was that, although he had come to Heidelberg with the intention of spending the rest of his life most usefully in advancing the affairs of Christ's kingdom, he was hindered by ill health and accomplished less than he wished. He was answered that it is a great thing for the Church's sake to lift up pure hands to God, to offer godly prayers and doxologies [δοξολογίας], and publicly and privately to give thanks to God for spiritual and bodily blessings; and that in this respect both he and other godly men greatly benefit the Church, even when, because of ill health, they cannot perform their other duties.

units.la: Decessit piè, placideque vt nouistis, 2 Maij, manè, intra quintam & sextam: ac verè ijs annumerari potest, de quibus dictum est: Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriuntur: quoniam requiescunt à suis laboribus.
units.tr: He died piously and peacefully, as you know, on 2 May, in the morning, between five and six o'clock. He may truly be counted among those of whom it is said: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, for they rest from their labours."

units.la: Reliquit idem ingenij monumenta non contemnenda, venusta & pia Poëmata, quæ propter elegantiam magnis illis viris, Domino Camerario & Philippo probata fuerunt: sed certo consilio hactenus suppressa: quæ si bonis & doctis annuentibus per hæredes edi aliquando poterunt, eruditæ elegantiæ studiosis non iniucunda vel inutilia fore putantur.
units.tr: He also left behind monuments of his talent that are not to be despised: charming and pious poems, which, on account of their elegance, were approved by those great men, the lord Chamberlain and Philip; but they have hitherto been kept back by deliberate decision. If, with the approval of learned and good men, they can at some time be published by his heirs, they are thought not to be unpleasant or useless to students of refined elegance.

units.la: Hæc sunt, Magnificè & Illustris Domine Rector, clarissimi Doctores & Professores, nobiles generosi, cæterique studiosi Iuuenes, quæ de Doctore Friderico VVidebramo mihi visum est dicere. Est enim mihi & illius & aliorum defunctorum amicorum cogitatio dulcis: (vt cum Seneca loquar) quia habui illos non tanquam amissurus, sed præmissurus: amisi autem & præmisi illos, tanquam habeam.
units.tr: These are the things, Magnificent and Illustrious Rector, distinguished Doctors and Professors, noble and well-born men, and other young students, which it seemed right to me to say concerning Doctor Friedrich Widebram. For the thought of him and of my other departed friends is sweet to me; (to speak with Seneca) because I had them not as those who would lose them, but as those who would send them ahead; yet I have lost and sent them ahead, as though I still possessed them.

units.la: Quòd si, sententia beati Ambrosij, officium humanitatis defuncto collatum, præstantissimum est: Officium autem humanitatis est, ei qui piè, iustè, temperanter vixit (vt noster VVidebramus) virtutis testimonium perhibere: equidem eximio humanitatis officio me defunctum esse; ac mihi candidorum hominum candida iudicia, neutiquam defutura, non iniuria persuadeo.
units.tr: But if, according to the saying of the blessed Ambrose, the duty of humanity shown to the dead is most excellent, and the duty of humanity is to bear witness to the virtue of one who lived piously, justly and temperately (as our Widebram did), then I am persuaded, not without reason, that I have discharged an outstanding duty of humanity towards the departed, and that the fair judgments of fair-minded men will by no means be lacking to me.

units.la: Quod reliquum est, Deo gratias ago, quòd Doctori VVidebramo dedit, vt bonum certamen certaret, cursum consummaret, fidē retineret; ac eundem precor, vt nobis quoque det, vt in offenso pede per mundi huius tenebras, ad coelestem lucem alacres contendamus, duce & auspice Christo Iesu Domino nostro; ut re ipsa experiamur, hunc omnipotentem, veracem Dei Filium in carne patefactum, in Spiritu iustificatum, nobis & in vita & in morte esse lucrum.
units.tr: As for the rest, I give thanks to God that he granted Doctor Widebram to fight the good fight, to finish the course, and to keep the faith; and I pray the same God to grant us also, that, stumbling-footed through the darkness of this world, we may press on eagerly towards heavenly light, with Christ Jesus our Lord as leader and guide; so that we may experience in deed that this almighty, true Son of God, manifested in the flesh and justified in the Spirit, is gain to us both in life and in death.

units.la: DIXI. CARMINA FVNEBRIA. DE OBITV CLARISS. VIRI POETAE LAVDATISSIMI, Dn. FRIDERI- CI VVIDEBRAMI, S. THEOLOGIAE Doctoris, placidè in Christo defuncti Heidelbergæ: TELLVRIS ET FOSSORIS διαλογισμός.
units.tr: I have spoken. Funeral poems. On the death of the most distinguished and most praised poet, Friedrich Widebram, Doctor of Sacred Theology, who died peacefully in Christ at Heidelberg: a dialogue between the Earth and the Gravedigger.

units.la: CVr propriam fossor violas malefidè parentem, Rumpere cur huius claustra ligone paras? Nonne aliud fuerat, quo caca cadauera ponas Hospitium, an me non tristior extat humus? Antè salutiferas locus hic proferre solebat Herbas, nunc tetri plenus odoris erit. Antè puellaris flores hîc cura legendi: Tollere nunc erit hinc ossa retecta labor.
units.tr: Why do you plot, gravedigger, to break open with your mattock the mother who is your own, and faithlessly so? Could you not have found some other lodging where you might lay your blind corpses? Or is the ground not sadder to me? Once this place used to bring forth healing herbs; now it will be full of foul stench. Once it was a girl's delight to gather flowers here; now it will be a labour to lift from here the bones laid bare.

units.la: Quid doleas, nescis: fundis sine mente querelas: Nunc iras, grates, sat scio, deinde feres. Non mihi communis temerè pia membra parentis Rumpere, sed semper mens decorare fuit.
units.tr: You do not know what you grieve for; you pour out complaints without thought. Now you will bear anger, and then thanks, I know well. It was never my intent to rashly break open the pious limbs of a common mother, but always to adorn them with the mind.

units.la: CARMINA
units.tr: POEMS

units.la: Nunc quoque quicquid ago, non dedecus, asque tua spectato Commoda, per longos non moritura dies. Ergo age, neue diu mentem suspendito nostram, Quid sibi vult istud, dic bone fossor, opus?
units.tr: Even now, whatever I do, I look to your interests, which bring no disgrace and will not die through the long days. Come then, and do not keep my mind long in suspense. Tell me, good gravedigger, what is this work meant to be?

units.la: Esse vir doctrinae fama super aethera notus, Sedem defuncto hic hospitium q; paro. Si ferres famâ totum cantata per orbem Balsama, non tibi tam gloria magna foret, Quàm fuerit pia membra senis tumulata fouenti De quo quàm fari pauca, tacere iuuat. Hei mihi quantus erat, quàm multis saepè petitus, Quem Panoris molli sola fouebit humo! Hei mihi quàm multi busto hoc posse multa reperto Secla, loco hoc, dicent, ô VVidebrame iaces. I nunc atque nouas porrò contexe querelas, Dum facio vt summus sic tibi crescat honos.
units.tr: A man of learning, known by fame beyond the heavens, I am preparing a resting place here for the dead man. Even if you carried through the whole world the balm that fame has sung of, it would not be as great a glory for you as the pious limbs of the old man entombed here are for the one who cherishes them. About him it is pleasant to say little and to keep silent. Alas, how great he was, and how often sought out by many, whom the lone soil of Panor will softly cherish! Alas, how many, at this tomb, will say that the ages could have held much... here you lie, Widebram. Go now, and weave new laments further, while I make it so that such honour grows for you.

units.la: Nescieram: quaeso nugis ignosce rogantis: Tanti hominis semper molliter ossa tegam.
units.tr: I did not know. I beg you, forgive the trifles of one who asks. I shall always cover the bones of so great a man gently.

units.la: Ἐπιτάφιος [?] EIVSDEM.
units.tr: Epitaph [Ἐπιτάφιος] of the same author.

units.la: Hic memorande senex posse mille pericula vitae, Sanctae Dei miles iam VVidebrame cubas. Alter eras Simeon: qui te non nouit, is illum Cogitet, effigies optima vatis eras. Ille quidem manibus tenerum portauit Iesum: Cura tibi hunc lingua ferre animoq; fuit. Heidelberga sibi te tam citò luget ademptum: Sed superi gaudent, Thariadaeq; sinus.
units.tr: Here lies, memorable old man, you who could withstand a thousand dangers of life, holy soldier of God, Widebram. You were another Simeon. Whoever did not know you, let him consider that you were the finest image of a prophet. He indeed carried the tender Jesus in his arms; care for him was in your tongue and in your soul. Heidelberg mourns you, snatched from it so quickly; but the gods rejoice, and the bosom of Thariadae.

units.la: FVNEBRIA.
units.tr: FUNERAL TRIBUTES.

units.la: Annus & dies obitus.
units.tr: The year and day of death.

units.la: Vix bene finierant Maiæ sua festa Kalendæ,Astra habet arte potens & pietate senex.
units.tr: Scarcely had the Kalends of May finished their festivities when the old man, mighty in skill and in piety, took his place among the stars.

units.la: I. Rybinius E. Pol. manibus senis pientissimi sibique amicissimi gratificans ἐγχαρτε.
units.tr: I. Rybinius E. Pol., gratifying the shade of the most pious old man and of his dearest friend [ἐγχαρτε].

units.la: MEMORIAE D. FRIDERICI VVIDE-BRAMI, OPTIMI ET THE- OLOGI, & Poetæ.
units.tr: IN MEMORY OF D. FRIEDRICH WIDEBRAM, EXCELLENT THEOLOGIAN AND POET.

units.la: SVmmo poëtæ æquum est poëtas carmine Memori parentare; Ipse quod facerem libens; Sed metuo, olores inter anser ne strepam, Video & voluntati esse vires impares.
units.tr: It is fitting that poets should honour a fellow poet with song, and I would gladly do so myself. But I fear that among swans I may hiss like a goose, and I see that my powers are unequal to my will.

units.la: Laudes viri ergo tanti ego forte ingeni Ne deteram culpa (ipsius requirerent Nam VVidebrami venam, & argutam chelyn) Tantum à Deo hoc optabo donum Ecclesiæ, Felix ut illa ita, atque concors floreat, Ne quando VVidebrami opem desideret.
units.tr: So, lest I spoil the praises of so great a man of talent (for they would demand Widebram's vein and his keen lyre of me), I will ask only this gift from God for the Church: that she may flourish happy and united, and never have to long for Widebram's help.

units.la: V. A. P.
units.tr: V. A. P.

units.la: EPITAPHIVM FRIDERICI VVIDEBRAMI D. THEOLOGI, Scriptum à DAVIDE PAREO SILESIO.
units.tr: EPITAPH OF FRIEDRICH WIDEBRAM, DOCTOR OF THEOLOGY, written by DAVID PAREUS OF SILESIA.

units.la: FRiderici hac tegit vrna VVidebrami Doctoris pia membra : quem Nariscis
units.tr: This urn covers the pious limbs of Friedrich Widebram, Doctor, whom Nariscus

units.la: D. Pesnicum
units.tr: Pesnicum, D. (Doctor)

units.la: CARMINA
units.tr: VERSES

units.la: Tractus eò per vim, quod vel præsaga futuri Tractus eò per vim, quod vel præsaga futuri Mens foret, aut fugeret grande laboris onus. Nec mora, cum reliquis, sic Electore iubente, Nomine Doctoris claruit, inde crucis; Dogmata quod nollet Torgæ composita probare, Scripturis sacris esse aliena ratus. Postea tamen infractus paulatim carcere, ijsdem Applicuit certa conditione manum. Liber ab hoc ternis Neoburgi substitit annis, Quo miserum voluit Dux remanere loco. Tandem cum fixum nollet deponere sensum, Saxonicos, iussus linquere, liquit agros. Vxoremque trahens secum, natosque tenellos Nassouij petijt rura vetusta soli. Doctrinaque pia Decianis pauit in agris Commissum, fermè per duo lustra, gregem. Inde Eitelbergam venit, pars vna Senatus, Omnia quo Princeps templa scholasque regit. Sævitia hîc morbi postea annum est mortuus, inter Suffultas solida spesque fideque preces, Quas numeris solitus fuerat comprendere doctis, Vt probat Isaidæ nobile regis opus, Æmula complectens Romanæ carmina linguæ, Siue Siberetuis, siue Eobane tuis. Tres nati, totidem natæ cum matre, rogarunt Versibus appingi tale Epigramma meis. Iure exoptasti cælestia gaudia votis Fridrice, in terris dum miser hospes eras. Altera tristitiæ vitæ pars, prima laborum, Morborumque tibi tertia tota fuit: Sudasti iuuenis, vir flesti, iamque senescens Ex vitio stomachi deficientis, obis
units.tr: He was dragged there by force, though his mind, foreseeing the future, would have fled the great burden of toil. Without delay, with the others, at the Elector's command, he gained the name of Doctor and then the cross, because he would not approve the doctrines drawn up at Torgau, which he judged alien to the holy Scriptures. Afterwards, however, worn down little by little by prison, he put his hand to the same things on a certain condition. Freed from this, he remained three years at Neuburg, in the wretched place where the Duke wished him to stay. At last, since he would not lay aside his fixed opinion, he was ordered to leave, and he left the Saxon fields. Taking his wife and tender children with him, he sought the old fields of the land of Nassau. There, in the Dietz fields, he fed with sound teaching the flock committed to him, for nearly two lustra (about ten years). Thence he came to Eitelberg, one part of the consistory, where the prince governs all the churches and schools. Here, after a year, he died of the violence of disease, amid prayers supported by solid hope and faith, which he was accustomed to set down in learned metres, as the noble work of Isaidas proves, embracing in rivalry the poems of the Latin tongue, whether those of Siberetus or your own, Eobanus. Three sons and as many daughters with their mother asked that such an epigram be added to my verses. Rightly did you long for heavenly joys with your prayers, Friedrich, while you were a wretched sojourner on earth. The second part of your life was sorrow, the first was toil, and the third was wholly made up of diseases. As a youth you sweated, as a man you wept, and now, growing old, from the failing of your stomach, you died.

units.la: FVNEBRIA.
units.tr: FUNERAL ELEGY.

units.la: Ad tempus, nobis: Domino tua vita superstes, Est & erit: credens interijsse nequit. Insertus vita viti qui palmes adhæret, Non metuit falcem, mors violenta, tuam.
units.tr: For a time, to us: your life, Friedrich, survives with the Lord, and will survive; the one who believes cannot perish. Grafted into the vine of life, the branch that clings to it does not fear your sickle, violent death.

units.la: Simon Stenius Lomacensis.
units.tr: Simon Stenius of Lomacz.

units.la: ALIVD.
units.tr: ANOTHER.

units.la: VVidebramus amicis loquitur.
units.tr: Widebram speaks to his friends.

units.la: Quam mihi terra dedit patriam male fida, repulsum Egit in exilium. In cœlis pia quæ mansit me patria, tristi Eximit exilio. O nati, ô coniunx, meus, ô vos, sanguis, amici Sistite nunc lacrymas. Vt mundo nasci mors est: sic prorsus, eidem, Est noua vita, mori.
units.tr: The land, faithless to me, gave me a homeland and then drove me back and forced me into exile. The pious homeland that remains for me in heaven releases me from sad exile. O my children, O my wife, O you my blood and my friends, now stop your tears. As to be born into the world is death, so for the same man to die is a new life.

units.la: IN OBITVM FRIDERICI VVIDEBRAMI THEOL. D. scriptum ab EBERHARDO DEDEKINO BREMENSI.
units.tr: ON THE DEATH OF FRIEDRICH WIDEBRAM, DOCTOR OF THEOLOGY, written by EBERHARD DEDEKIND OF BREMEN.

units.la: FAma fidem fecit moriturus vt ardua Cygnus Aptet in argutos ora, trahatq;, modos: Scilicet à Zephyris vbi forte remurmuret aër, Spiritum𝍐 alto in gutture formạt opus.
units.tr: Rumour gives assurance that the dying swan fits its beak to sweet, piercing strains and draws them out. Of course, when the air happens to murmur with the western breezes, it shapes its song from breath in its lofty throat.

units.la: CARMINA FVNEBRIA.
units.tr: FUNERAL SONGS.

units.la: Qui viuens igitur se nulla in carmina soluit, Dulcia sub media carmina morte canit!
units.tr: He who, living, therefore dissolves himself into no song, sings sweet songs even in the midst of death!

units.la: Ista subest rebus Naturae abscondita virtus, Mortis & haec nostrae symbola cygnus habet.
units.tr: This hidden power lies beneath the things of Nature, and the swan bears these tokens of our death.

units.la: Sic audita senis vox est Simeonis ad aras, Sic tua in algenti vox V Videbrame thoro.
units.tr: So was heard the voice of old Simeon at the altar; so was your voice, Widebram, on your bed of chill.

units.la: Scilicet afflatum caelo se sensit vterq;,Et sibi promissum vidit vterq; DEVM.
units.tr: Both of them, assuredly, perceived that they were inspired from heaven, and both saw God who had been promised to them.

units.la: Ille oculis & corde simul: qua parte beatiQuisq; sumus; tantum hic non dubitante fide.
units.tr: The one saw him with his eyes and at the same time with his heart, in whichever part we are blessed; the other only with heart, yet without doubting faith.

units.la: Nil oculis vidisse iuuat, si pectore nolis: Corde suo Christum qui videt, ille videt.
units.tr: It avails nothing to have seen with the eyes if you are unwilling with the breast: he who sees Christ with his heart, he sees.

units.la: Nec caeli tantum hinc metuas bonus interuallum, Quo nunc à nobis carne Redemtor abest.
units.tr: Nor, good man, should you fear this great interval of heaven, by which the Redeemer is now absent from us in the flesh.

units.la: Namq; suo praesens immenso numine, regnumVi patriâ exercet victor vbiq; suum.
units.tr: For being present by his immense power, he rules his kingdom, and as victor he exercises his dominion everywhere.

units.la: Nec tibi simpliciter quoq; corpus abesse putabis, Membra suo capiti si sacra Flamma liget.
units.tr: Nor will you think that the body is simply absent from you, if the sacred Flame binds your members to its head.

units.la: Inde mori sanctis dulce est, omnisq; sepulcri, Terror in aeternae gaudia lucis abit.
units.tr: Hence it is sweet for the saints to die, and the terror of every grave passes into the joys of eternal light.

units.la: Nempe Deo vitam si quis moriente recepit, Huic mors in viuo fit noua vita Deo.
units.tr: Indeed, if anyone has received life from God while dying, for him death becomes a new life in God who lives.

units.la: Hic si se videat promissa in pace resolui, Dulcia cygnaeo carmina more canat:
units.tr: If he sees himself being released in peace as promised, he sings sweet songs in the manner of the swan:

units.la: Grata quies tumulus, quibus est fundata supernè, Statq; fide in passo spes animosa DEo.
units.tr: "The tomb is a welcome rest, on which a rest has been founded from above, and a hopeful hope stands in faith in God who suffered."
